title: Peperonata
subtitle: Italian slow-cooked sweet pepper and tomato stew
excerpt: Southern Italy's great pepper dish: red, yellow, and orange peppers slowly braised with tomatoes, onion, and garlic in olive oil until completely soft, sweet, and deeply concentrated. Excellent warm, at room temperature, or cold.

recipe.sourceNotes: Peperonata is a traditional Italian braised pepper dish found throughout southern Italy, particularly in Campania and Sicily, with variations across the entire peninsula. The dish is made by slowly cooking sweet peppers (mixed red, yellow, and orange for colour and sweetness) with tomatoes, onion, and garlic in abundant olive oil until the peppers are completely tender and the flavours are concentrated and sweet. It is one of the most versatile dishes in Italian cooking: served as an antipasto, as a side dish with meat or fish, as a pasta sauce, or on bruschetta. The slow cooking transforms the peppers from crisp to silky and removes much of their bitterness, producing a gentle sweetness. Like most braised vegetable dishes, peperonata is better the next day.

content.text: Use a mixture of red, yellow, and orange peppers for the best flavour and appearance; green peppers are more bitter and less suitable. The dish needs time; rushing the cooking produces peppers that are still slightly firm and lack the melting sweetness of a properly made peperonata. This is a dish that benefits from being made ahead.
Heat the olive oil in a large, wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 10 minutes until soft and golden. Add the garlic and cook for 2 more minutes.

Add the peppers and stir to coat in the oil. Cook over medium-low heat for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until starting to soften. Add the tinned tomatoes and season with salt and pepper. Simmer for 20 to 25 minutes until the peppers are completely soft and the sauce has thickened.
Stir in the red wine vinegar. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Remove from the heat and scatter with torn basil. Serve warm, at room temperature, or cold.
